slides.text:
Continuum of social entrepreneurs in six descending degrees of altruism:
(1) The person who attempts to innovatively profit society alone, at risk of personal loss. Creative philanthropist willing to martyr self for the benefit of others.
(2) The person who attempts to innovatively profit
society alone, at risk of foregoing personal profit.
(3) The person who attempts to innovatively profit
society by profiting himself, at risk of incurring personal loss.

slides.title: social entrepreneurship continuum
slides.text:
social entrepreneurship continuum
(1) Community-based enterprises: Charitable organizations that are engaged in carrying out their social goals involving risk.
Bridge the gap in the services
Grace Orchard School in Singapore: Two churches collaborated with to start a government-aided private school for children with special educational needs.
The government funds the project with the location and the recurrent cost while the alliance partners provide the management, recruit volunteers and consider long-term financial support.

slides.title: social entrepreneurship continuum
slides.text:
social entrepreneurship continuum
(2) Socially responsible enterprises: Banyan Tree Gallery (BTG) is an
extension of the social consciousness of the Banyan Tree Holiday Resorts (BTHR) business.
BTHR developed environmentally sensitive luxury boutique resorts that are steeped in Asian traditions.
Its Phuket resort was a disused 400-hectare tin mining site described in a 1977 United Nations report as being ‘too severely ravaged’ to sustain development.
The Banyan Tree team preserved the remaining trees, planted 800 new ones and transformed the site to include six lagoons stocked with fish, tiger prawns, shrimp and other animals.
BTG was founded in 1994 when triangular cushions made by female Thai villagers were incorporated into Banyan Tree Phuket.

slides.text:
Social entrepreneurship continuum
(3) Social Service Industry Professionals: Northern Leaf Communications
(NLC), a PR firm specializing in Internet design, corporate design, marketing communications and the launching of events.
It uses the charity angle to approach companies after their first successful collaboration with the Children’s Cancer Foundation in 1995.
NLC helped in raising funds & generating awareness of charity’s work.
NLC’s success in managing this project enabled it to pitch for new projects for non-profit organizations.
At present, its main clients are about twenty non-profit organizations.
NLC offers an attractive proposition to its clients that couples NLC’s business objective with their clients’ social goals.

(4) Socio-economic or dualistic enterprises: Successfully incorporate
the ‘social’ in their mission statement or they have the dual objective of not only earning profits but also of conducting non-profit making activities for the community.
Transnational Recycling Industries Pte Ltd. specializing in paper materials, old newspapers & corrugated, computer & waste paper.
It gathers recyclable materials from households and selling these to a recycling company, with part of profits used for community projects.
As the cost of the materials is zero, and only operational costs are incurred in collecting the materials, Transnational benefits greatly if the quantity of collected material increases.

slides.title: hybrid organizations
slides.text:
hybrid organizations
Primarily pursue a social mission but rely significantly on
commercial revenue to sustain operations.
Traditional businesses usually think of their consumers as
customers, whereas traditional nonprofits think of their consumer base as beneficiaries.
Hybrids, however, break this traditional customer-beneficiary
dichotomy by providing products and services that, when consumed, produce social value.

slides.title: 3 types of legal structures for hybrids
slides.text:
3 types of legal structures for hybrids
The L3C (Low Profit Ltd Liability) is a variant of an LLC, designed primarily to enable companies to access investment from tax-exempt sources such as private foundations.
The Benefit Corporation is a corporate form to consider a designated social purpose and corresponding social impact alongside financial analysis in making strategic and tactical business decisions.
The Flexible Purpose Corporation, which has passed in California and Washington (where it is called the Social Purpose Corporation), requires boards and management to agree on one or more social and environmental purposes with shareholders.
Program-related investments (PRIs), enable private foundations to invest through equity, debt, or a mixture of both—have increased access to capital for US hybrids.

bullets.text: The L3C (Low Profit Ltd Liability) is a variant of an LLC, designed primarily to enable companies to access investment from tax-exempt sources such as private foundations.
The Benefit Corporation is a corporate form to consider a designated social purpose and corresponding social impact alongside financial analysis in making strategic and tactical business decisions.

The Flexible Purpose Corporation, which has passed in California and Washington (where it is called the Social Purpose Corporation), requires boards and management to agree on one or more social and environmental purposes with shareholders.
Program-related investments (PRIs), enable private foundations to invest through equity, debt, or a mixture of both—have increased access to capital for US hybrids.

slides.text:
In the UK, a Community Interest Company (CIC) provides tax benefits to hybrids that agree to limit their distributions to investors.
A CIC, once given governmental approval, has its assets “frozen” and designated for general community benefit.
Investors can receive capped dividends on their investment, but the principal is never retrieved.
Tax laws were not built for organizations that pursue social and financial value. Still, the emergence of new hybrid legal structures will likely encourage increased hybrid activity. What remains to be seen is which legal structures will be the best fit for hybrids.

slides.title: Impact Investing
slides.text:
Impact Investing
Traditional early stage equity financing methods used by the venture capital industry are not suited to social ventures.
Investors who embrace the same dual objectives as hybrid entrepreneurs are needed. Impact investors who are comfortable with hybrid models and their blend of social value creation and commercial revenue.
The global impact investing market will be at least $500 billion within the next decade, most hybrid entrepreneurs still experience difficulty in raising capital.
Solving this challenge will require changes in mindsets of investors, who will have to accept a return that range from a below market to market rate, as well as improved capital placement structures.

slides.title: Critique:
slides.text:
Critique:
One view of social value is exemplified by Harvard University economist Robert Barro.
“By any reasonable calculation Microsoft has been a boon for society,” Barro argued, “and the market value of its software greatly exceeds the likely value of Mr. Gates’ philanthropic efforts.”
Barro helpfully differentiates the market value of the goods sold by Microsoft from the social value derived from those sales: “Suppose that a copy of a new version of Windows sells for $50 (and is typically charged as part of the price of a personal computer). Microsoft’s revenue from Windows would then equal $50 multiplied by the number of copies consumers snap up.
Microsoft’s earnings are the revenue less production and development expenses. But that’s not the social value. That comes from the increase in productivity created when businesses and households use the software.
The social benefit equals the value of the extra product, less the total paid for the software.” By this definition, every entrepreneur is a social entrepreneur and every market transaction creates social value, the bigger the better.

Microsoft’s revenue from Windows would then equal $50 multiplied by the number of copies consumers snap up.

Microsoft’s earnings are the revenue less production and development expenses. But that’s not the social value. That comes from the increase in productivity created when businesses and households use the software.

The social benefit equals the value of the extra product, less the total paid for the software.” By this definition, every entrepreneur is a social entrepreneur and every market transaction creates social value, the bigger the better.

slides.text:
James A. Phills Jr., Kriss Deiglmeier, and Dale T. Miller, in “Rediscovering Social Innovation”, Stanford Social Innovation Review, fall 2008, take a strikingly different view of social value. They broaden the domain of inquiry from social entrepreneurship to “social innovation”, which they define as follows:
“A novel solution to a social problem that is more effective, efficient, sustainable, or just than existing solutions and for which the value created accrues primarily to society as a whole rather than private individuals.”
This view of value creation puts a great deal of weight on the difference between social and private problems to be solved on one hand, and the social and private value created as a consequence of novel solutions on the other.
They define social value as: “The creation of benefits or reductions of costs for society—through efforts to address societal needs and problems—in ways that go beyond the private gains and general benefits of market activity.”
